genealogy.name: The Genealogy of Christ
genealogy.keyText: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
genealogy.story: Matthew opens his gospel not with the birth but with the family tree: forty-two generations from Abraham to Christ, arranged in three equal spans of fourteen. The genealogy is a confession of faith — it declares that this child is the one the whole of Israel’s history was reaching toward. Four women appear by name: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah — all outsiders or sinners, signs from the very first line that the Messiah comes for all people.
genealogy.fathers: Matthew begins with the genealogy because he writes for Jews, and nothing would so delight them as to learn that Christ was born of their own forefathers. Yet even here the Gentile women appear as a sign: the grace of Christ surpasses the boundaries of the old covenant from the very first page.
genealogy.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily III
hot: Three times fourteen
Three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the Exile, from the Exile to Christ — three epochs of salvation history, and Christ the goal of all three.
The four women
Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba — all outsiders or sinners by human reckoning, yet honoured in the genealogy of the Lord. Grace exceeds all human boundaries.
The name ‘Christ’
The list ends with ‘Jesus, who is called Christ.’ The whole of Israel was, unknowingly, praying for this name.

annunciation.name: The Annunciation
annunciation.keyText: Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.
annunciation.story: Before Mary and Joseph had come together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. Joseph, being a just man, resolved to put her away quietly. But the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream: ‘Fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.’ The child was to be called Jesus — God saves — fulfilling Isaiah’s ancient word: Emmanuel, God with us.
annunciation.fathers: The angel appeared to Joseph in a dream because Joseph was a man of remarkable virtue and simplicity of heart. The name Jesus contains the whole gospel: he shall save his people from their sins. This is why he came — not to be served but to save.
annunciation.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily IV
hot: The angel in the dream
Joseph receives the annunciation not waking but in a dream: the divine word enters the stillness of the heart.
The name JESUS
Hebrew Yeshua: God saves. The name is not a decoration but a declaration of mission.
Emmanuel, God with us
Isaiah is fulfilled: God does not send a messenger but comes himself, and the humanity he takes is forever his own.

magi.name: Adoration of the Magi
magi.keyText: And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and... presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.
magi.story: Wise men from the East followed a rising star to Jerusalem, troubling Herod and all the city. Sent on to Bethlehem, they found the child with Mary his mother, fell down and worshipped him, and opened their treasures — gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home another way.
magi.fathers: The wise men were not troubled at the poverty of the birthplace. They saw no purple hangings, no royal throne — only a manger and a cave. Yet they fell down and worshipped. Their three gifts were a confession: gold for a King, frankincense for God, and myrrh for one who would die and be buried.
magi.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily VI
hot: The moving star
A star that travels and stops over the cave: the heavens themselves announce the King, the first preachers of the gospel.
The three gifts
Gold, frankincense, and myrrh — confessing kingship, divinity, and the death to come.
The enthroned Mother
Mary is shown as a living throne, presenting the Child outward to the world; she is the Theotokos, the God-bearer.

nativity.name: The Nativity of Christ
nativity.keyText: Out of Egypt have I called my son.
nativity.story: After the Magi departed, an angel warned Joseph to flee into Egypt; they remained there until Herod’s death, fulfilling the prophet’s word. When Herod saw he had been outwitted he slaughtered the male children of Bethlehem — the Holy Innocents, the first martyrs of Christ. Warned again by an angel, Joseph brought the family back and settled in Nazareth. The Nativity icon gathers the whole mystery in one image: cave, manger, star, angels, shepherds, the Holy Family, and the Magi.
nativity.fathers: Thy Nativity, O Christ our God, hath shone forth the light of knowledge upon the world; for by it, they that worshipped the stars were taught by a star to adore Thee, the Sun of Righteousness. O Lord, glory to Thee!
nativity.fathersAttr: Troparion of the Nativity of Christ, Tone 4
nativity.fathersExtra: On this day the Virgin giveth birth to Him Who is above all being; and the earth offereth a cave to the Unapproachable One. Angels and shepherds give glory, and the Magi journey with a star: for unto us there is born a young Child, the pre-eternal God.
hot: The cave and the star
Not a palace but a cave: Christ enters the darkest place to fill it with light. The star sends its ray straight down, joining heaven and earth.
The Holy Innocents
The slaughter of the innocents is part of the Nativity story: the powers of the world rage against the King they cannot control.
The Holy Family on the road
Joseph leads Mary and the child into Egypt by night: the Lord of all becomes a refugee, sharing the road of the hunted.

forerunner.name: St John the Forerunner
forerunner.keyText: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
forerunner.story: John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness of Judaea, clothed in camel’s hair, his food locusts and wild honey, preaching repentance and the nearness of the kingdom. Jerusalem and all Judaea came to be baptized in the Jordan, confessing their sins. He warned of the wrath to come, and pointed beyond himself to One mightier, whose sandal he was not worthy to carry.
forerunner.fathers: Why did John dwell in the wilderness? That he might not be entangled with the affairs of common life, nor softened by custom, but might come among the people with all the authority of one set apart. The wilderness was his school; solitude was his training.
forerunner.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily X
hot: The angel’s wings
John is given wings because ‘angel’ means messenger: he is the herald sent before the face of Christ.
The axe at the root
An axe laid to the foot of a tree: a summons to bear the fruit of repentance, not merely profess faith.
Camel’s hair and girdle
His rough garment marks the ascetic and prophet: he belongs not to the palace but wholly to God.

theophany.name: The Baptism of Christ
theophany.keyText: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
theophany.story: Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John, who at first refused. As he came up from the water, the heavens opened; the Spirit descended like a dove; and the Father’s voice was heard: ‘This is my beloved Son.’ The feast is named Theophany — the showing-forth of God — for here the Holy Trinity is revealed.
theophany.fathers: When Thou wast baptized in the Jordan, O Lord, the worship of the Trinity was made manifest; for the voice of the Father bare witness unto Thee, and the Spirit, in the form of a dove, confirmed the truthfulness of His word. O Christ our God, glory to Thee!
theophany.fathersExtra: The sinless One enters the waters not to be cleansed but to cleanse them, sanctifying all water and our own baptism in it. The Spirit descended as a dove, for it was fitting that the Spirit, who is meekness itself, should appear in the form of the most peaceful of birds.
theophany.fathersExtraAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XII
hot: The dark water
The Jordan is painted almost as a watery abyss: Christ’s descent foreshadows his descent into death and the drowning of sin.
The dove and the ray
The Spirit descends as a dove upon a ray from the opened heavens, completing the revelation of the Holy Trinity.
Angels with veiled hands
Angels stand on the bank, hands covered in cloth: even the highest beings stand in awe at the mystery.

temptation.name: The Temptation of Christ
temptation.keyText: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
temptation.story: After his baptism, Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness and fasted forty days. The devil tempted him three times — to turn stones to bread, to cast himself from the Temple, to gain the world’s kingdoms by worship. Each time Jesus answered with Scripture; at the third refusal the devil departed and angels ministered to him.
temptation.fathers: Why was He led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted? That He might teach us that after baptism we need not expect rest, but conflict. He overcame by the word of Scripture, that when the enemy comes we must answer him from that same armory.
temptation.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XIII
hot: The barren wilderness
Bare rock and emptiness: the place where there is nothing but God and the soul, and the contest is fought and won.
The tempter, small and dark
The devil is shown diminished before the Word made flesh: his power is real, but before Christ already broken.
The ministering angels
After the temptations are refused, the angels draw near to serve: the reward shown to all who endure.

calling.name: The Calling of the Fishermen
calling.keyText: Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
calling.story: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon called Peter and Andrew casting their net, and called them. Immediately they left their nets and followed. Going further he saw James and John with their father mending nets; he called them also, and at once they left boat and father and followed.
calling.fathers: He saw them at their work and called them — not from idleness but from labour, for God loves those he finds busy. They left everything immediately — nets, boat, father — and followed. From their small nets He was sending them to gather the whole world.
calling.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XIV
hot: The net and boat
The tools of their former life left at once: the very moment of the great leaving, an image of conversion.
Christ’s outstretched hand
The Lord stands on the land and calls across the water: the gesture of calling that goes out to every generation.
Andrew the First-called
Andrew, the first to follow, is honoured as Protokletos — the First-called — the pattern of all who leave all to follow.

beatitudes.name: The Sermon on the Mount
beatitudes.keyText: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
beatitudes.story: Seeing the multitudes, Jesus went up into a mountain and taught them the Beatitudes — blessing the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. He named his disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world.
beatitudes.fathers: See where He begins: not with riches nor outward greatness, but with humility of soul — ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit.’ For he who has cut out the root of pride has slain at one stroke the whole multitude of evils that grow from it.
beatitudes.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XV
hot: The mountain
Christ teaches from a mountain as Moses received the Law on Sinai: the new Law of the Beatitudes is given by God himself.
The hand raised in blessing
The teaching gesture of Christ is also a blessing: his words do not merely instruct but bestow the blessedness they name.
Salt and light
‘Ye are the salt of the earth... the light of the world.’ The disciples are sent to season and illumine all the nations.

lordsprayer.name: The Lord’s Prayer
lordsprayer.keyText: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
lordsprayer.story: On the mountain Christ taught his disciples not to give alms, pray, or fast for the praise of men, but in secret before the Father who sees in secret. And he gave them the prayer that bears his name — ‘Our Father which art in heaven’ — the pattern of all Christian prayer, which the Church prays at every service to this day.
lordsprayer.fathers: Consider the honour God has given us: He commands us to call God Father, and so to know ourselves His children. And He says ‘Our Father,’ not ‘My Father,’ that we might pray for the whole body of the Church and never seek our own things only.
lordsprayer.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XIX
hot: ‘Our Father’
We are taught to say ‘Our,’ not ‘My’: prayer binds the whole Church into one family, and no one prays alone.
In secret
Christ sets prayer in the hidden chamber of the heart, that the Father who sees in secret may reward openly.
Daily bread
The prayer asks only for this day’s bread: dependence on God, freeing the heart from anxious hoarding for tomorrow.

wisebuilder.name: The Wise and Foolish Builders
wisebuilder.keyText: Whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock.
wisebuilder.story: Christ ended the Sermon on the Mount with warnings: enter by the narrow gate; beware false prophets known by their fruits; not everyone who says ‘Lord, Lord’ will enter, but he who does the Father’s will. The wise man builds on rock and stands in the storm; the foolish builds on sand and falls. The people were astonished, for he taught as one having authority.
wisebuilder.fathers: He did not say ‘He that heareth’ only, but ‘He that heareth and doeth.’ For hearing is not enough; and even the house on the rock is not proven secure until the rains and floods come. Trials do not overthrow the one founded on obedience — they reveal him.
wisebuilder.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXIV
hot: The house on the rock
The rock is the doing of Christ’s words; only obedience can bear the weight of the storms to come.
The narrow gate
Two ways are set before every hearer: the broad road to destruction and the narrow gate to life.
Teaching with authority
Unlike the scribes who quoted others, Christ teaches from himself: the Lawgiver speaks, and the crowds are astonished.

storm.name: Christ Stilling the Storm
storm.keyText: Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.
storm.story: As they crossed the sea, a great tempest arose and the boat was covered with waves, while Jesus slept. They woke him crying, ‘Lord, save us: we perish.’ He rebuked their little faith, then rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. The men marvelled: ‘What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?’
storm.fathers: He slept to give place to their fear, that the miracle might be more clearly seen; and rising, by a word He stills the sea, that they might learn He is the same Lord who in the beginning set bounds to the waters.
storm.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXVIII
hot: The sleeping Christ
In his humanity he truly sleeps; in his divinity he commands the sea. The one boat holds both the weakness and the power of God.
The rebuked waves
He ‘rebukes’ the sea as a master a servant: the One who set its bounds at creation commands it by a word.
The little boat
The Fathers see the boat as the Church, tossed by the storms of the world yet never sunk, for Christ is within her.

paralytic.name: Healing the Paralytic
paralytic.keyText: The Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house.
paralytic.story: They brought to Jesus a man sick of the palsy. Seeing their faith, he said, ‘Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee.’ When the scribes accused him of blasphemy, he answered by healing the body as proof of his power to forgive: ‘Arise, take up thy bed.’ The man rose and departed, and the multitudes glorified God.
paralytic.fathers: He heals the soul first and the body after, that we might learn the worse disease is sin. And He proves the unseen forgiveness by the seen healing: making the lesser miracle the witness of the greater.
paralytic.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXIX
hot: The bed carried away
He who was carried now carries his own bed: a healing so complete the man’s burden becomes his witness.
Soul before body
Christ forgives sins before he heals the limbs: the deepest paralysis is that of the soul.
The doubting scribes
The scribes’ objection becomes the very occasion for Christ to reveal his authority to forgive.

matthew.name: The Calling of St Matthew
matthew.keyText: He saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.
matthew.story: Passing by, Jesus saw Matthew the tax-collector at the receipt of custom and said, ‘Follow me.’ He arose and followed, and made a feast with many publicans and sinners. When the Pharisees objected, Christ answered: ‘They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick... I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.’
matthew.fathers: Mark the power of Him who called, and the obedience of him who was called. He did not ask for delay nor say ‘Let me first settle my accounts,’ but left all and followed. This same Matthew, once a gatherer of taxes, became a gatherer of nations.
matthew.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXX
hot: The tax table
Matthew is shown at the customs table, symbol of a life bound to money: from it Christ calls him to a new account.
The summoning hand
Christ’s outstretched hand and single word are enough; the icon paints the instant of leaving all behind.
The Evangelist’s book
The tax-collector becomes an Evangelist, shown with the gospel he would write — the fruit of his calling.

jairus.name: The Daughter of Jairus
jairus.keyText: But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.
jairus.story: A ruler knelt, saying his daughter was dead, but that Christ’s touch would restore her. On the way a woman with an issue of blood twelve years was healed by touching the hem of his garment. Arriving, Jesus put out the mourners, took the girl by the hand, and she arose. And he went about healing, moved with compassion for the multitudes, who were as sheep without a shepherd.
jairus.fathers: He took her by the hand, that He might give strength by the touch of His flesh; and He called death a sleep, to teach us that to Him the dead are only sleeping, awaiting His word to awaken them.
jairus.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXXI
hot: The hand that raises
Christ takes the dead girl by the hand: the touch of the life-giving flesh of God awakens her as from sleep.
The hem of the garment
The woman healed by touching his hem shows that even the edge of Christ’s humanity overflows with the power of God.
‘Not dead, but sleeping’
Christ names death a sleep, robbing it of its terror: the dead only await the word that will wake them.

twelve.name: The Sending of the Twelve
twelve.keyText: Freely ye have received, freely give.
twelve.story: Jesus called his twelve disciples, gave them authority over unclean spirits and every disease, and sent them to the lost sheep of Israel to preach that the kingdom was at hand. He charged them to go without gold or provision, to fear not those who kill the body, and to confess him before men. Whoever received them received him; and the one who endured to the end would be saved.
twelve.fathers: He sends them as sheep in the midst of wolves — not to be devoured, but to conquer by patience; for it is the part of wolves to do violence, and of sheep to suffer it. Yet He bids them be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.
twelve.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXXII
hot: The Twelve
Twelve apostles for the twelve tribes: Christ founds a new Israel, sending out the first preachers of the kingdom.
Sheep among wolves
They go without staff or gold, defenceless: their only weapon is the gospel, their only armour patience.
‘Freely give’
What they received as a gift they must give as a gift: the grace of God is never sold.

yoke.name: Come Unto Me
yoke.keyText: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
yoke.story: After rebuking the cities that would not repent, Christ rejoiced that the Father had revealed these things to babes. Then he spoke words the Church has never ceased to treasure: ‘Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you... for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.’
yoke.fathers: He calls not this man or that, but all who are in toil, in sorrow, in sin. And the rest He gives is not idleness but a yoke — yet a yoke that is easy, for it is borne with Him, and love makes every burden light.
yoke.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXXVIII
hot: The open hands
Christ is shown with hands open in invitation: the call goes out to all, with no condition but the willingness to come.
The easy yoke
A yoke joins two to share a load. Christ’s yoke is easy because he bears the heavier end.
Rest for the soul
The rest he promises is peace in the midst of labour: the soul at rest in God even while the hands still work.

sabbath.name: Lord of the Sabbath
sabbath.keyText: For the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath day.
sabbath.story: When the Pharisees accused his disciples of plucking grain on the Sabbath, and him of healing a withered hand, Christ answered that he desired mercy and not sacrifice, and that the Son of man is Lord of the Sabbath. He healed the man’s hand, declaring it lawful to do good on the Sabbath day.
sabbath.fathers: The Sabbath was made for man, to give him rest and turn his mind to God; it was not made to forbid mercy. Therefore the Lord of the Sabbath heals upon it, showing that the law of love is its true fulfilment.
sabbath.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XXXIX
hot: The withered hand restored
Christ heals on the Sabbath to show that the day of rest is for works of mercy, not against them.
‘Mercy, not sacrifice’
He quotes Hosea: God desires a merciful heart above all ritual observance. Love is the law’s fulfilment.
Lord of the Sabbath
The One who rested on the seventh day of creation declares himself its Master: the Sabbath serves him.

sower.name: The Parable of the Sower
sower.keyText: But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit.
sower.story: From a boat Jesus taught the crowds in parables. A sower went forth to sow: some seed fell by the wayside and was devoured, some on stony ground and withered, some among thorns and was choked, and some on good ground and bore fruit a hundredfold. He explained that the seed is the word of the kingdom, and the soils are the hearts that hear it.
sower.fathers: See the generosity of the sower: he does not pass by the rock, nor the thorns, nor the trodden path, but scatters his seed on every kind of ground. For the word of God is offered to all alike; the difference is not in the seed but in the soul that receives it.
sower.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XLIV
hot: The four soils
Wayside, rock, thorns, good ground: the one word of God meets four kinds of heart, and only the last bears fruit.
The generous sower
The sower casts seed even where it may not grow: God offers his word freely to all, withholding it from none.
The hundredfold harvest
The good soil yields thirty, sixty, a hundredfold: the heart that keeps the word is fruitful beyond measure.

kingdom.name: Parables of the Kingdom
kingdom.keyText: The kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
kingdom.story: Jesus likened the kingdom to many things: wheat and tares left to grow till the harvest; a tiny mustard seed that becomes a great tree; leaven hidden in meal; treasure hidden in a field; a pearl of great price for which a merchant sells all; and a net gathering fish of every kind. The kingdom is hidden, small, and precious beyond all things.
kingdom.fathers: The kingdom is like leaven: small in quantity, yet it changes the whole lump. So the gospel, though it seemed weak and few at first, has leavened the whole world. And it is like a pearl, for which the wise man gladly sells all: he loses nothing, but gains everything.
kingdom.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XLVII
hot: The mustard seed
The smallest of seeds becomes a tree: the kingdom begins hidden and weak, and grows to shelter all the nations.
The pearl of great price
The merchant sells all for one pearl: the kingdom is worth the whole of a life, and he who gives all loses nothing.
The wheat and tares
Wheat and weeds grow together till the harvest: the Church holds saints and sinners until God’s final separation.

beheading.name: The Beheading of St John
beheading.keyText: And he sent, and beheaded John in the prison.
beheading.story: Herod had imprisoned John the Forerunner for rebuking his unlawful marriage. At Herod’s birthday feast, the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him, and at her mother’s prompting asked for John’s head on a platter. Grieved but bound by his oath, Herod beheaded John in the prison. His disciples took up the body and buried it, and went and told Jesus.
beheading.fathers: John died for the truth, rebuking sin even at the cost of his head; and his death is more glorious than any throne. The Forerunner who pointed to the Lamb followed him also into death.
beheading.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XLVIII
hot: The platter
The Baptist’s head upon a dish is the cost of speaking truth to power: the icon does not hide what sin will do.
The prison
John dies unseen, at the whim of a feast: yet the Church remembers him while the king is forgotten.
The buried body
His disciples bury him and go to tell Jesus: the Forerunner precedes the Lord even into the grave.

feeding5.name: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
feeding5.keyText: And he took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples.
feeding5.story: When the crowds followed Jesus into a desert place, he had compassion and healed their sick. As evening came, with only five loaves and two fishes, he looked up to heaven, blessed and broke them, and gave to the disciples to distribute. Five thousand men, besides women and children, ate and were filled, and twelve baskets of fragments remained.
feeding5.fathers: He looked up to heaven before He brake the bread, to teach us that the gifts of the earth come from the Father. And He gave the loaves to the disciples to distribute, that we might learn He does His works through the hands of His Church.
feeding5.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XLIX
hot: The blessing of the loaves
Christ looks up and blesses before breaking: the Fathers see in it a foreshadowing of the Eucharist.
The twelve baskets
Twelve baskets remain for the twelve apostles: the bounty of God always exceeds the need.
The hands of the disciples
Christ feeds the multitude through the disciples’ hands: he works his miracles through his Church.

walking.name: Christ Walking on the Water
walking.keyText: And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?
walking.story: After the feeding, Jesus sent the disciples ahead and went up the mountain to pray alone. In the night the boat was tossed by waves, and he came walking on the sea. Peter walked toward him on the water, but seeing the wind he feared and began to sink, crying, ‘Lord, save me.’ Jesus caught him; the wind ceased; and they worshipped him as the Son of God.
walking.fathers: As long as Peter looked to Christ, the water bore him up; but when he turned his eyes to the wind, he began to sink. So it is with us: faith fixed on the Lord walks upon the deep. Yet even then the cry ‘Lord, save me’ is heard, and the hand is stretched out at once.
walking.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily L
hot: Christ upon the sea
He treads the waves as on dry land: the Creator walks upon the deep he made.
Peter sinking
Peter walks while he looks to Christ and sinks when he looks at the wind: an icon of every soul’s faith and fear.
The outstretched hand
‘Immediately’ Christ catches the sinking Peter: the hand of God reaches the one who cries out, even mid-fall.

canaanite.name: The Canaanite Woman
canaanite.keyText: O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt.
canaanite.story: After disputing with the Pharisees about tradition and true defilement, Jesus withdrew to the coasts of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman cried out for her demon-troubled daughter. Though he seemed at first to refuse, testing her, she persisted in humility: ‘Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.’ He marvelled: ‘O woman, great is thy faith,’ and her daughter was healed that hour.
canaanite.fathers: He delayed, not from unwillingness, but to draw out the treasure hidden in her soul. Had He granted her at once, we should not have known her faith. She, refusing to be put off, won by humility what she sought.
canaanite.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LII
hot: The kneeling woman
A Gentile and outsider kneels in persistent prayer: her humility becomes the model of how to pray and not lose heart.
‘The crumbs’
She turns her low place into a plea: even the crumbs of Christ’s grace are enough to heal.
‘Great is thy faith’
Christ praises her faith above that of Israel: the kingdom is opened to all who believe.

feeding4.name: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
feeding4.keyText: I have compassion on the multitude... and I will not send them away fasting, lest they faint in the way.
feeding4.story: On a mountain by the Sea of Galilee, great crowds came with their sick, and Jesus healed them, so the multitude glorified the God of Israel. Moved with compassion lest they faint, with seven loaves and a few small fish he gave thanks, broke, and fed four thousand men besides women and children; and seven baskets of fragments were taken up.
feeding4.fathers: Again He gives thanks first, that we might never take bread without remembering the Giver. And He says, ‘I have compassion’ — for His miracles flow not from display but from mercy: He cannot bear to send the hungry away.
feeding4.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LIII
hot: ‘I have compassion’
The miracle is born of mercy: Christ will not send the hungry away faint, and his power always serves his compassion.
The seven loaves
Seven loaves and seven baskets: the number of fullness, the sign of a God whose provision is complete.
The mountain
As on the mount of the Beatitudes, Christ teaches and feeds from a height: the bread of his word and of his hands together.

confession.name: The Confession of Peter
confession.keyText: Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.
confession.story: At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asked, ‘Whom say ye that I am?’ Peter answered, ‘Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ Jesus blessed him, for flesh and blood had not revealed it but the Father. Then he began to foretell his suffering, death, and resurrection, and taught that whoever would follow him must take up his cross.
confession.fathers: Peter’s confession was not learned from men but given by the Father; and on this faith the Church is built and cannot fall. From this hour the Lord begins to speak of the Cross, for the confession of His glory must be joined to the confession of His suffering.
confession.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LIV
hot: The question
‘Whom say ye that I am?’ stands at the centre: the whole gospel turns on each soul’s answer.
The confession
Peter confesses Christ as Son of the living God: the rock of faith on which the Church is built.
The first word of the Cross
Immediately after the confession of glory, Christ foretells his Passion: there is no crown without the Cross.

transfiguration.name: The Transfiguration
transfiguration.keyText: And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.
transfiguration.story: Six days later Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain and was transfigured: his face shone as the sun, his garments white as light. Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with him. A bright cloud overshadowed them and the Father’s voice said, ‘This is my beloved Son... hear ye him.’ The disciples fell on their faces in awe.
transfiguration.fathers: Thou wast transfigured on the mount, O Christ God, revealing Thy glory to Thy disciples as far as they could bear it. Let Thine everlasting light shine forth also upon us sinners, through the prayers of the Theotokos. O Giver of light, glory to Thee.
transfiguration.fathersExtra: He was transfigured, not receiving what He was not, but revealing to His disciples what He was; opening their eyes and giving sight to the blind. The light shone forth from within, for He is Himself the unapproachable Light.
transfiguration.fathersExtraAttr: St Gregory Palamas, Homily on the Transfiguration
hot: The uncreated light
Christ’s shining is not a borrowed light but the eternal radiance of his Godhead, shown as much as they could bear.
Moses and Elijah
The Law and the Prophets stand beside Christ: all of Scripture bears witness that he is its fulfilment.
The disciples fallen down
Peter, James, and John fall on their faces: the proper posture of the soul before the glory of God.

lostsheep.name: The Lost Sheep
lostsheep.keyText: Doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and goeth into the mountains, and seeketh that which is gone astray?
lostsheep.story: When the disciples asked who is greatest, Jesus set a child among them: unless they become as little children they cannot enter the kingdom. He warned against despising the little ones, and told of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one that wandered, rejoicing more over it than over those that never strayed.
lostsheep.fathers: See the love of God for man: He calls the wanderer not lost beyond hope, but a sheep to be sought; and He rejoices more over the one found than over the many safe. He measures not by number but by love.
lostsheep.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LIX
hot: The one and the ninety-nine
The shepherd leaves the many to seek the one: God’s love is not arithmetic, and no single soul is expendable.
The sheep on the shoulders
The Good Shepherd carries the found sheep home: an image of Christ bearing lost humanity upon himself.
The little child
Christ sets a child in the midst: humility and smallness, not greatness, are the door of the kingdom.

servant.name: The Unforgiving Servant
servant.keyText: Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? ...Jesus saith unto him... Until seventy times seven.
servant.story: Teaching on forgiveness, Jesus told of a servant forgiven a vast debt by his king, who then seized a fellow-servant for a tiny sum and cast him into prison. The king delivered the unmerciful servant to the tormentors. ‘So likewise shall my heavenly Father do, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.’
servant.fathers: Consider how great a debt God forgives you, and how small the debt your brother owes — ten thousand talents against a hundred pence. If you will not forgive so little, you cast away your own pardon; for the measure you give is the measure you will receive.
servant.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXI
hot: The great debt cancelled
The king forgives an unpayable sum: the image of God’s mercy toward each sinner.
The hundred pence
The servant chokes a fellow over a trifle: our grievances are tiny beside the mercy we have received.
‘From your hearts’
Forgiveness must be from the heart, not the lips: withheld mercy forfeits our own.

children.name: Christ Blessing the Children
children.keyText: Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.
children.story: After teaching on marriage and faithfulness, little children were brought to Jesus that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked those who brought them, but Jesus said, ‘Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.’ And he laid his hands on them and blessed them.
children.fathers: He sets the child before us for its simplicity — its freedom from malice, vainglory, and envy. He bids us be not childish in understanding, but childlike in innocence; for to such the kingdom belongs.
children.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXII
hot: The blessing hands
Christ lays his hands on the children: the God who stoops to the smallest and least.
The rebuked disciples
The disciples would keep the children away; Christ overrules them: none are too little for him.
‘Of such is the kingdom’
The child’s simplicity and trust are the pattern of all who would enter the kingdom.

richman.name: The Rich Young Man
richman.keyText: If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor... and come and follow me.
richman.story: A young man asked what he must do to have eternal life. Told to keep the commandments, he said he had kept them all. Jesus said, ‘If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor... and come and follow me.’ But he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. Then Jesus said it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom, but with God all things are possible.
richman.fathers: It was not the having of riches that condemned him, but the being held by them. He went away sorrowful because he was a slave, and his wealth was his master. The soul that owns nothing is richer than the one whom possessions own.
richman.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXIII
hot: The young man’s sorrow
He goes away grieved: the tragedy of a soul that loves the gift more than the Giver.
‘Sell and give’
Christ asks not only generosity but freedom: to be loosed from what we own so we may follow unburdened.
The eye of the needle
‘It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle’: riches are a heavy weight at the narrow gate.

vineyard.name: The Labourers in the Vineyard
vineyard.keyText: So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.
vineyard.story: Jesus likened the kingdom to a householder who hired labourers at dawn, and others at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. At evening he paid them all the same, beginning with the last. Those hired first complained, but he answered, ‘Is thine eye evil, because I am good?’ So the last shall be first, and the first last.
vineyard.fathers: God does not reckon by the length of labour but by the love of the worker. The one who comes at the eleventh hour, if he comes with his whole heart, is not behind the one who bore the heat of the day. For the wage is grace, not payment; and grace is given, not earned.
vineyard.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXIV
hot: The eleventh hour
Those hired last receive the same wage: no one who turns to God, however late, comes too late for his mercy.
The equal wage
All receive the same denarius: salvation is a gift given in full to each, not a payment scaled to labour.
‘Is thine eye evil?’
The grumbling of the first warns against envy of God’s generosity to others.

entry.name: The Entry into Jerusalem
entry.keyText: Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.
entry.story: As they drew near Jerusalem, Jesus rode in upon a donkey, fulfilling the prophet’s word: ‘Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass.’ The multitudes spread their garments and palm branches in the way, crying, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ And the whole city was moved, asking, ‘Who is this?’
entry.fathers: In confirming the common Resurrection, O Christ God, Thou didst raise up Lazarus from the dead before Thy Passion. Wherefore we also, like the children, bearing the symbols of victory, cry to Thee, the Vanquisher of death: Hosanna in the highest; blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord.
entry.fathersAttr: Troparion of the Entry into Jerusalem, Tone 1
hot: The humble donkey
The King comes not on a war-horse but on a donkey: a meekness that conquers not by force but by love.
Palms and garments
The crowds spread palms and cloaks — a king’s welcome; yet within days the same city will cry ‘Crucify.’
The children’s Hosanna
Children cry Hosanna: the Church sees in them the pure praise the proud could not offer.

temple.name: The Cleansing of the Temple
temple.keyText: My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
temple.story: Entering the temple, Jesus cast out all who bought and sold, overturned the tables of the money-changers, and declared, ‘My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.’ The blind and lame came to him there and were healed, while children cried Hosanna. He taught in parables, and the chief priests sought to seize him.
temple.fathers: He shows His authority over the temple as its Lord, driving out those who made the house of prayer a market. And straightway the blind and lame come to Him there and are healed: where the buyers and sellers are cast out, there mercy enters in.
temple.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXVII
hot: The overturned tables
Christ overthrows the money-changers’ tables: holy zeal, the one time the gentle Lord acts with force.
‘A house of prayer’
The temple is for prayer, not profit: an icon of the heart, which must be swept of its idols.
Healing in the temple
Once the traders are gone, the blind and lame are healed: mercy fills the space that greed had occupied.

wedding.name: The Marriage Feast
wedding.keyText: For many are called, but few are chosen.
wedding.story: Jesus likened the kingdom to a king who made a marriage for his son and sent servants to call the invited, who would not come. So he sent into the highways to gather all he found, both bad and good, and the wedding was furnished with guests. But one man without a wedding garment was cast out: ‘For many are called, but few are chosen.’
wedding.fathers: The feast is ready, the call gone out to all — but one comes without the wedding garment, and is cast out. For it is not enough to be called; we must be clothed, putting on the new life of grace. The garment is the deeds and the love that befit the King’s table.
wedding.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXIX
hot: The open invitation
Servants gather all from the highways, good and bad: the call of the gospel goes out to every kind of person.
The wedding garment
One guest is cast out for lacking the garment: to accept the call is not enough; we must be clothed in grace.
The King’s son
The feast is the marriage of the King’s Son: the union of Christ with his Church, to which all are bidden.

commandment.name: The Greatest Commandment
commandment.keyText: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
commandment.story: The Pharisees and Sadducees tried to trap Jesus with questions of tribute, resurrection, and the law. Asked which is the great commandment, he answered: love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, soul, and mind; and the second is like it, to love thy neighbour as thyself. ‘On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.’ And no one dared ask him any more.
commandment.fathers: He joins the two commandments and will not separate them: love of God and love of neighbour are one garment, woven without seam. He who truly loves God cannot despise the one made in God’s image.
commandment.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXXI
hot: The two commandments
Love of God and of neighbour are inseparable: on these two the whole law and the prophets hang.
‘With all thy heart’
God asks not a portion but the whole: heart, soul, and mind given wholly to him.
The silenced questioners
After this answer none dared question him: divine wisdom puts to silence every attempt to trap the truth.

olivet.name: The Second Coming
olivet.keyText: They shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.
olivet.story: On the Mount of Olives, Jesus foretold the destruction of the temple and the signs of the end: wars, famines, false prophets, and the gospel preached to all nations. He spoke of the coming of the Son of man in glory and of the need to watch, for no one knows the day or hour. Be ready, like a faithful servant whom the master finds at his work.
olivet.fathers: He tells us the signs, yet hides the day, that we might watch always; for if we knew the hour, we should grow careless until it drew near. He leaves it unknown, that every hour might find us ready.
olivet.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXXVII
hot: The Son of man in glory
Christ will return not hidden as at Bethlehem but in glory on the clouds: the same Lord, now revealed to all.
The unknown hour
The day is hidden so that we may watch always: ignorance of the hour is given for constant readiness.
The faithful servant
Blessed is the servant found at his work: watchfulness is not fear but faithful labour.

virgins.name: The Ten Virgins
virgins.keyText: Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.
virgins.story: Jesus likened the kingdom to ten virgins who took their lamps to meet the bridegroom: five were wise and took oil, five were foolish and took none. While the bridegroom tarried they slept; at midnight the cry came. The foolish found their lamps going out, and while they went to buy oil the door was shut.
virgins.fathers: The oil is mercy and good works, which cannot be borrowed or bought at the last hour, but must be gathered through a whole life. The foolish virgins kept their virginity, but had no oil of love; so even the lamps of the chaste go dark without works of mercy.
virgins.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXXVIII
hot: The lamps
All ten carry lamps, but only five burn at midnight: outward profession without inner oil cannot meet the Bridegroom.
The oil
The Fathers read the oil as mercy and love, gathered over a lifetime and unable to be borrowed at the last hour.
The shut door
‘The door was shut’: a warning that there is a time of readiness which, once past, does not return.

talents.name: The Parable of the Talents
talents.keyText: Well done, thou good and faithful servant... thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things.
talents.story: A man travelling into a far country gave his servants talents — five, two, and one. The first two traded and doubled them and were praised; but the one who received a single talent buried it in fear, and was condemned as wicked and slothful, his talent given to the one who had ten.
talents.fathers: The talents are the gifts of God — to each according to his strength — and from each the same faithfulness is asked. He is condemned not for gaining less, but for gaining nothing; not for weakness, but for sloth. The buried gift is the gift refused.
talents.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXXVIII
hot: The entrusted talents
Each receives according to his ability: God gives differing gifts, but asks the same faithfulness of all.
The buried talent
The third servant is condemned for burying his gift: grace is given to be used, not hidden.
‘Enter into the joy’
The faithful are welcomed into their master’s joy: the reward of labour is communion with God.

judgment.name: The Last Judgment
judgment.keyText: Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
judgment.story: Christ foretold his coming in glory, when all nations shall be gathered and he shall separate them as a shepherd divides sheep from goats. To those at his right: ‘Come, ye blessed... for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat,’ for what was done to the least was done to him. To those at his left who did not: ‘Depart from me.’
judgment.fathers: See by what we are judged: not by fasting, nor by miracles, but by mercy — whether we fed the hungry, clothed the naked, visited the prisoner. Christ so joins Himself to the poor that He calls their hunger His own.
judgment.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXXIX
hot: The sheep and the goats
Christ divides all the nations: every life is finally weighed before him.
‘The least of these’
Christ identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger, the prisoner: mercy to them is mercy to him.
Judged by mercy
Not miracles nor knowledge but acts of love decide the judgment: the gospel’s final word is compassion.

supper.name: The Mystical Supper
supper.keyText: Take, eat; this is my body... For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.
supper.story: As the Passover drew near, the chief priests plotted, Judas agreed to betray him, and a woman anointed him for his burial. At the supper Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it: ‘Take, eat; this is my body’; and the cup: ‘this is my blood of the new testament, shed for many.’ He foretold his betrayal and Peter’s denial, and they sang a hymn and went out.
supper.fathers: Of Thy Mystical Supper, O Son of God, accept me today as a communicant; for I will not speak of the Mystery to Thine enemies, neither will I give Thee a kiss as did Judas; but like the thief will I confess Thee: Remember me, O Lord, in Thy kingdom.
supper.fathersAttr: Pre-Communion hymn of the Divine Liturgy
supper.fathersExtra: He gave them His own Body and Blood, that they who eat might be joined to Him. This is the supper that has never ended: the same Christ who broke bread that night breaks it still upon every altar.
supper.fathersExtraAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXXXII
hot: The bread and the cup
‘This is my body... this is my blood’: the institution of the Eucharist, the supper continued in every Liturgy.
The reclining Twelve
The apostles gather close at the table: the first communion of the Church, gathered around her Lord.
Judas reaching in
Judas is shown reaching toward the dish: the betrayer at the holy table, a warning to approach with a pure heart.

gethsemane.name: The Agony in the Garden
gethsemane.keyText: O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
gethsemane.story: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus took Peter, James, and John and began to be sorrowful unto death. He prayed three times, ‘O my Father... not as I will, but as thou wilt,’ while the disciples slept. Then Judas came with a multitude and betrayed him with a kiss; one drew a sword, but Jesus healed and rebuked, and all the disciples forsook him and fled.
gethsemane.fathers: He prayed, ‘Let this cup pass,’ to show the truth of His human nature, which shrinks from death; and He added, ‘not as I will, but as Thou wilt,’ to teach us obedience. In His agony He sanctifies our own fear, and shows the way through it: the surrender of the will.
gethsemane.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily LXXXIII
hot: The cup
‘Let this cup pass’: Christ’s true human dread of death, and the surrender of his will to the Father.
The sleeping disciples
Peter, James, and John sleep while he prays: the weakness of the flesh beside the watchfulness of the Lord.
The kiss of Judas
The betrayer’s kiss turns the sign of love into the instrument of treachery: the Passion begins.

crucifixion.name: The Crucifixion
crucifixion.keyText: Truly this was the Son of God.
crucifixion.story: At Golgotha they crucified Jesus between two thieves, casting lots for his garments, mocking him. From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covered the land. He cried, ‘My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?’ and yielded up his spirit. The veil of the temple was torn, the earth quaked, and the centurion confessed, ‘Truly this was the Son of God.’
crucifixion.fathers: Today He who hung the earth upon the waters is hung upon the Cross. He who is King of the angels is arrayed in a crown of thorns. Let all creation tremble; let us worship Him in silence, for He suffers willingly for our salvation.
crucifixion.fathersAttr: Antiphon 15 of the Matins of Holy Friday
crucifixion.fathersExtra: The Cross is not the defeat of Christ but His throne. He reigns from the tree; He stretches out His hands to gather the scattered children of God; and in dying He tramples death. Therefore we venerate the Cross as the weapon of peace and the tree of life.
crucifixion.fathersExtraAttr: From the hymns of the Holy Cross
hot: The Cross as throne
Christ reigns from the Cross: the icon shows him not writhing but at peace, the King enthroned upon the tree of life.
The skull at the foot
A skull beneath the Cross marks Golgotha and Adam’s grave: the blood of the new Adam falls upon the old.
The centurion’s confession
‘Truly this was the Son of God’: the first confession at the Cross comes from a Gentile soldier.

burial.name: The Burial of Christ
burial.keyText: And laid it in his own new tomb... and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.
burial.story: As evening came, Joseph of Arimathea begged the body of Jesus from Pilate, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb hewn in the rock, rolling a great stone to the door. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sat watching. The chief priests, remembering his words, sealed the stone and set a guard.
burial.fathers: He who is everywhere present is shut within a tomb, and the Life of all lies lifeless, that He might fill the grave with His presence and rob it of its power. The stone is sealed and the watch is set — yet they guard in vain, for they cannot keep the Author of life among the dead.
burial.fathersAttr: From the hymns of Holy Saturday
hot: The new tomb
Christ is laid where none had lain: as he was born of a virgin womb, so he is buried in a virgin grave.
The linen shroud
Joseph wraps him in clean linen: the swaddling-bands of Bethlehem return as burial-cloths, the manger become a tomb.
The sealed stone
The guard and the seal are set in vain: human power cannot keep the Lord of life in the grave.

resurrection.name: The Resurrection
resurrection.keyText: He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay.
resurrection.story: As the first day of the week dawned, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to the tomb. An angel descended, rolled back the stone, and sat upon it, his face like lightning: ‘Fear not... He is not here: for he is risen, as he said.’ They departed with fear and great joy, and Jesus himself met them, saying, ‘All hail.’ But the guards were bribed to say his body was stolen.
resurrection.fathers: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and upon those in the tombs bestowing life!
resurrection.fathersExtra: The angel rolled away the stone not to let the Lord out — for He had already risen — but to show the women that the tomb was empty. So the stone that sealed despair becomes the seat of the messenger of joy: death is overthrown, and the grave is now a gate.
resurrection.fathersExtraAttr: From the Paschal hymns of the Church
hot: The empty tomb
The angel shows the women the place where he lay: the icon proclaims not a corpse but an absence.
The myrrh-bearing women
The women who came to anoint a body are the first witnesses and first preachers of the Resurrection.
The stone rolled back
The stone of the grave becomes the angel’s seat: what sealed death is overthrown, and the tomb becomes a gate to life.

commission.name: The Great Commission
commission.keyText: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
commission.story: The eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had appointed, and worshipped him. Jesus came and spoke: ‘All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost... and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.’
commission.fathers: He sends fishermen and tax-gatherers to teach all nations, that the power might be seen to be God’s and not man’s. And He ends not with a command only but with a promise: ‘I am with you always.’ The gospel that begins with ‘Emmanuel, God with us’ ends with the same word.
commission.fathersAttr: St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew, Homily XC
hot: The mountain
As the gospel’s great moments unfold on mountains, so the last: the disciples are sent from a height to the whole earth.
‘All nations’
The mission is universal: the gospel breaks every boundary of people and place.
‘I am with you always’
The gospel that opened with ‘God with us’ closes with the same promise: Christ remains with his Church to the end of the age.
